title: What is antidisestablishmentarianism? | THE LONGEST WORDS

entries.note: Said to be the longest word ever written: about 189,000 letters listing the chemicals that make up [[see:titin]], and a reading of it takes nearly two hours.
A protein, and a much more concise name for the thing that the enormous chemical word [[see:methionylthreonylthreonylglutaminylalanyl…]] spells out.
An inherited condition affecting the thyroid, given as an example of long English words built from scientific components.
A long chemical name for a gas that, according to the hosts, is used as a fire repellent on submarines and aircraft.
The adverb form of electroencephalograph, a device that records brain waves.
Linguists' term for building words by adding pieces to the end, as German, Sanskrit, Ancient Greek, Finnish and Hungarian do, while English prefers separate words.

entries.translation: Association for subordinate officials of the main electric services of the Danube steamship company
entries.note: A famous hypothetical German compound: technically possible but not really used, it packs a whole English phrase into one word.
A real 63-letter German word for a law on beef labelling; it was German word of the year in 1999 and the law lapsed in 2013.
The Icelandic volcano that baffled newscasters; its name breaks down into island, mountain (related to [[same-root:fell]]) and glacier, and its double L sounds like T.
One of the island names, said to come from the Vikings, that end in the same 'ey' (island) element found in [[see:Eyjafjallajökull]].
One of the island names ending in the 'ey' (island) element found in [[see:Eyjafjallajökull]].
One of the island names ending in the 'ey' (island) element found in [[see:Eyjafjallajökull]].
One of the island names ending in the 'ey' (island) element found in [[see:Eyjafjallajökull]].
English word for a mountain, related to the 'fjalla' (mountain) element of [[same-root:Eyjafjallajökull]].
A fictional dish in [[see:Assemblywomen]], made of 25 Greek words for cooking methods, flavours and ingredients such as sharks, pigeons, hares, crabs and honey.
[[see:Aristophanes]]'s comedy of 391 BC, which features the absurdly long name of a fictional dish.
A 19th-century double negative for opposition to [[see:disestablishmentarianism]]; it became famous as a long word through [[see:Gloria Lockerman]]'s 1955 TV spelling.
The Victorian movement to undo the establishment of the [[see:Church of England]] as the official state church; related movements existed in Ireland and Scotland.
Set up by [[see:Henry VIII]] so that he could divorce [[see:Catherine of Aragon]]; it is the 'establishment' in [[see:antidisestablishmentarianism]] and remains the official church.
Founded the [[see:Church of England]] to break with Rome so that he could divorce [[see:Catherine of Aragon]].
A 12-year-old Black girl who spelled [[see:antidisestablishmentarianism]] on [[see:The $64,000 Question]] in 1955, became a sensation and later a schoolteacher.
The 1950s game show on which [[see:Gloria Lockerman]] spelled [[see:antidisestablishmentarianism]]; it was cancelled after a scandal over coached contestants.
A sister show to [[see:The $64,000 Question]], where [[see:Gloria Lockerman]] spelled a whole sentence and tied with a boy to split $32,000.
A major show that featured [[see:Gloria Lockerman]] and received hostile letters from viewers because she was Black.
This show mentioned [[see:antidisestablishmentarianism]] because of [[see:Gloria Lockerman]]'s cultural impact.
An actress, later famous for playing Helen Keller, who also appeared on [[see:The $64,000 Question]] and testified before Congress in the scandal.
The act of estimating something as worthless; an Eton coinage stringing together Latin words for trifles from William Lily's grammar, such as [[from:floccus]] (lock of wool) and [[from:nihil]].
An Eton-educated former MP who used [[see:floccinaucinihilipilification]] about the EU, the longest word ever said in the House of Commons.
An insult once used to describe [[see:Jacob Rees-Mogg]], which the hosts call fabulous.
A real medieval Latin word meaning the state of being able to achieve honours, used in [[see:Love's Labour's Lost]] as a joke about pretentious length.
A Shakespeare play that uses [[see:honorificabilitudinitatibus]] as a joke.
A word made up for one particular occasion or context; 'nonce' dates from the 1200s but is also a very offensive British insult.
A deliberately 101-letter [[see:nonce word]] from [[see:Finnegans Wake]] for the thunderclap at Adam and Eve's fall, made from words for thunder in many languages.

[[see:James Joyce]]'s work, which contains several ridiculously long words, including the thunderclap word [[see:bababadalgharaghtakamminarronnkonnbronntonnerronntuonnthunntrovarrhounawnskawntoohoohoordenenthurnuk]].
A word that appears only once in a given context; unlike a [[see:nonce word]], it needn't be coined for that occasion.
A made-up word for acting like a hyena, used as an example of a possible [[see:nonce word]].
Historically a word that boxed women in, it was ironically reclaimed in a TikTok meme by [[see:Jools Lebron]], which Jess discussed on BBC World Service.
A trans creator with a big personality who turned [[see:demure]] on its head in a humorous TikTok meme inspired by her retail-work experiences.
Rob noticed people using it a lot, apparently wrongly, as part of the same meme as [[see:demure]].
A 21-letter word built with prefixes and suffixes, usable in everyday life.
A 20-letter word that you might realistically use.
Another everyday long word, built from prefixes and suffixes.
Another everyday long word, built from prefixes and suffixes.
A suffix called the friend of every Scrabble player wanting to extend a word.
A suffix that can jokingly make almost anything long.
A recent, deliberately fanciful word for the fear of long words, built on [[from:sesquipedalia]]; the hippo and monstro parts are extra hyperbole.

entries.translation: a foot and a half long
entries.note: A Latin word for things a foot and a half long, genuinely applied to long words, perhaps evoking blackletter words stretched across medieval manuscript pages.
Given to using long words; a word for every word nerd's arsenal, with [[see:oligosyllabic]] as its antonym.
Having few syllables, an ironically long antonym of [[see:sesquipedalian]], from the prefix oligo- (few) shared with [[same-root:oligarchy]].
Rule by the few; it shares the prefix oligo- (few) with [[same-root:oligosyllabic]].
A 45-letter pseudo-scientific word coined by [[see:Everett M. Smith]] of the National Puzzlers' League, extending [[from:pneumoconiosis]] with ultra, microscopic and volcano; means [[see:silicosis]].
A short word meaning exactly the same as [[see:pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis]].
A real medical term for a lung condition caused by inhaling dust, from Greek words for lungs and dust; it gave [[gave:pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis]].
The longest accepted binomial name for an organism, a bacterium named after the Welsh village [[from:Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch]], where it was found in soil.
The Welsh village with a very long name, where the soil sample containing [[see:Myxococcus llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogochensis]] was found.
A dad joke: the longest word is smiles, because there is a mile between the first and last letters.
Rob's British metric version of the [[see:smiles]] joke.

entries.translation: seven hundred and seventy-seven thousand seven hundred and seventy-seven
entries.note: German writes numbers as single words, and adding an ordinal ending makes them longer still, so the longest possible word is effectively infinite.
Jess's married surname, made by mashing two surnames together rather than hyphenating them, as an example of [[see:portmanteauization]].
Offered as a nice long word for mashing names together instead of hyphenating them.
Hanging precariously, as if by a thread, from filament plus pendulous; homework for listeners.
Literally [[equivalent:navel-gazing]]; now used jokingly for self-absorption, but a real meditative practice in yoga and Eastern Orthodoxy, linked to the [[see:omphalopsychites]].
The everyday expression that [[equivalent:omphaloskepsis]] literally means.
The name later historians gave to monks on Mount Athos who were said to experience celestial joys while gazing at their navels.
Fond of or preoccupied with ants; with its -philous ending, it is also used scientifically for factors that help ant populations grow.
Means beautiful and is popular with word nerds, though Jess feels it sounds unpleasant enough to suggest something else.
